questions.question: What is the Go race detector and how do you use it?
questions.title: Race Detector
questions.direct_answer: go run/test -race instruments memory accesses and reports unsynchronized read/write pairs. Run in tests and CI — catches data races before production. No code changes needed.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: go run/test -race instruments memory accesses and reports unsynchronized read/write pairs. Run in tests and CI — catches data races before production. No code changes needed.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Enable with -race:

```bash
go test -race ./...
go run -race main.go
```

Executed on our buggy counter (100 goroutines, no lock):

WARNING: DATA RACE
Read at ... by main goroutine
Previous write at ... by goroutine 106

The complete diagnostic: lines, goroutines, stack traces.

What it detects: unsynchronized concurrent access with at least one write. What it does NOT: deadlocks, logical races, or races your tests never execute.

How it works: every memory access is instrumented to check happens-before edges — if two accesses to the same memory aren't separated by a sync primitive (mutex, channel, atomic), the race is reported.

The cost: ~2-10x slower, ~5-10x memory. That's why it's a TEST flag. The discipline: every CI pipeline runs go test -race.

The guarantee: NO false positives — if it reports a race, there IS a race. False negatives exist (paths your tests didn't trigger). A clean run proves the TESTED paths are clean, not all paths.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    W[go test -race] --> IN[instrument every access] --> CHK{happens-before edge?}
    CHK -->|no| R[report DATA RACE]
    CHK -->|yes| S[safe]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The implementation — vector clocks and shadow memory: the detector maintains a happens-before graph per goroutine (vector clocks). Every sync operation updates the clocks. Every memory access checks: does the other access's clock dominate mine (ordered → safe), or are they concurrent (race → report).

The shadow memory: for every 8 bytes of program memory, the detector tracks metadata — hence 5-10x memory. The instrumentation wraps every load/store — hence 2-10x CPU. These constants are why -race is a build mode.

The false-negative surface: the detector only sees interleavings your tests produce. A race on an untested path is invisible — a clean run means 'executed paths were clean.' The mitigation: tests that actually run concurrent scenarios (the N-goroutine counter test).

The relation to production: some teams run -race on canary/staging deployments for real traffic patterns. The usual boundary is test/CI — the cost is designed for it, and coverage discipline lives in the test suite's concurrency quality.
